latin.1638: LXXXI. Ad hoc varia respondent & comminiscuntur Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae; sed quorum vanitas statim appareat rem absque affectu & praejudicio pensanti & consideranti. Cardinalis Perronius per Religionem Angelorum intelligi non vult eam qua Angeli coluntur, sed potius eam quae ab Angelis tradita est; & eo nomine designari conjicit religionem Judaicam, seu ritus Mosaicos, quoniam aliis in locis lex a Paulo dicitur Ordinata per Angelos in manu Mediatoris. Ac proinde ex ejus mente Scopus Apostoli est Colossenses revocare a cultu Judaico, & Mosaicae legis ceremoniis. Adversus Regem Magnae Britan. lib. 5. cap. 6. Gal. 3.
latin.1639: LXXXII. Sed primum istud Perronii commentum plane novum est, & apud Christianos omnes ad ejus usque tempora inauditum. Nec enim veteres tantum, ut Origenes, Chrysostomus, Hilarius sub Ambrosii, Pelagius sub Hieronymi nomine, Theodoretus, Theophylactus & Oecumenius per Angelorum Religionem intelligunt eam cujus Angeli objectum essent; sed ne quidem ullus interpretum Ecclesiae Romanae, quo sensu Perronius, ante ipsum Pauli verba sumpsit. Neque etiam tanti Cardinalis authoritas doctissimis post eum in Ecclesia ista viris commentum illud probare potuit. Sed ab iis diserte tanquam inane rejectum est, ut inter alios a Petavio Jesuita Nobili Antiquario. Theol. dogm. Tom. 3. lib. 2. cap. 9. paragr. 16.
latin.1640: LXXXIII. Et certe non solum in Scriptura sacra nusquam lex Mosaica Angelorum θρησκεία Religio appellatur, sed nec hujus nomenclaturae exemplum ullum reperiri potest apud authores quoscunque sive profanos, seu Ecclesiasticos. Neque si usitata esset ejusmodi appellatio, isti Pauli loco accommodari posset. Cum enim Paulus in praecedentibus, Colossenses claris & disertis verbis, adversus impostorum Judaizantium fraudem abunde munierit, dicens Nemo vos judicet in cibo, aut in potu, aut in parte diei festi, aut Neomenia, aut Sabbatorum; quae sunt umbra futurorum, corpus autem Christi; quid attinebat rem eandem verbis illis obscuris & ambiguis repetere? Adde quod istos Angelorum religionis introductores Paulus affirmat ambulare in iis quae non viderunt, id est, pedem inferre in ea quae non norunt, & de incognitis garrire: quod optime quidem quadrat in cultores Angelorum, qui de Angelorum natura, ordinibus atque muneribus incomperta multa effutiunt: in addictos vero legi Mosaicae non convenit; cum disciplina Mosaica in sacris voluminibus accurate explicata, & omnibus qui eam noscere vellent exposita esset.
latin.1641: LXXXIV. Itaque alio recurrunt Scholae Romanae Theologi, ut Ecclesiae suae fidem & praxin adversus tam disertam Apostoli legem tueantur. Eo vero redit plurium & Doctiorum solutio, Apostolum non damnare religiosum cultum & invocationem Angelorum, vel Sanctorum; sed solum cultum & adorationem falsam, superstitiosam & idololatricam. Qualem docuisse dicunt Simonem Magum, & Cerinthum, ac utriusque Discipulos. Sed istud merum est eorum figmentum, quod in Apostoli verbis atque doctrina fundamentum nullum habet. Nec enim Apostolus ullo pacto docet aut innuit esse quandam Angelorum θρησκείαν, seu religionem piam atque licitam, se autem solum damnare illam quae immodica est & idololatrica. Sed simpliciter & in genere damnat religionem Angelorum. Proinde quicunque fuerint veterum haereticorum circa Angelorum naturam, officia & cultum, errores, id non obstat quominus Pauli interdictum violent etiam illi qui hodie religioso cultu Angelos prosequuntur, & θρησκείαν quamcunque Angelis & Sanctis exhibent; quandoquidem Apostolus θρησκείαν Angelorum absolute prohibet; non vero eam dontaxat quam Simon vel Cerinthus illis detulisse dicuntur. Manifestum est autem illos Angelos & Sanctos θρησκεύειν qui eos colunt votis, precibus, hymnis, basilicis, oratoriis, festis, donariis, & omnis generis oblationibus, ut in Ecclesia Romana solenne est: & consequenter quod facit hac in parte Ecclesia Romana ab Apostolo damnari, non minus quam quod fecisse traditur, vel Simon, vel Cerinthus, aut si qui fuerint similes haeretici.
latin.1642: LXXXV. Regerunt Scholae Romanae Doctores quibuscunque ritibus & actibus Angeli & Sancti apud ipsos colantur, cultum illum divinum non esse: quoniam Angelos & Sanctos non ut Deos, sed ut Dei Ministros, & nostros apud Deum intercessores colunt: θρησκείαν autem seu Religionem esse cultum Deo proprium, & qui alicui ut Deo exhibetur. Sed ex ipso Apostoli textu satis colligi potest illos quos ibi arguit, & a quibus cavendum docet, non habuisse Angelos pro Diis, sed pro summi Dei nunciis & Ministris, nostrisque apud Deum Mediatoribus & deprecatoribus, quod arguit ipsum Angelorum nomen quod illis tribuebant: Angelus enim nuncium significat. Adde quod seductores illi Christianos se profitebantur, & colebant Angelos sub humilitatis praetextu, quasi indigni essent, qui immediate ad Deum accederent, & propterea opus apud ipsum haberent Angelorum mediatione & intercessione. Unde satis liquet ipsos Angelos coluisse cultu quodam subalterno, infra illum quem summo Deo deberi putabant: Adeoque, juxta Apostoli mentem, Angelis θρησκείαν deferre etiam eos qui colunt Angelos cultu quodam inferiori, nec Angelos pro Diis habent.
latin.1643: LXXXVI. Quaenam autem esset istorum pseudochristianorum, qui veteribus Angelici dicti sunt, erga Angelos Religio, colligere possumus ex Synodo Laodiceno: cujus reperitur hic Canon Codici Canonum Ecclesiae Universae insertus. Quod non oportet Christianos Ecclesiam Dei relinquere, & abire, & Angelos nominare, & Congregationes facere, quod est prohibitum. Quid vero sit, ex mente istius concilii, Angelos nominare, explicat Theodoretus in Epistolam ad Colossenses scribens, & locum illum quem urgemus exponens. Qui legem, inquit, defendebant, eos etiam ad Angelos colendos inducebant, dicentes legem fuisse per eos datam: Mansit autem perdiu hoc vitium in Phrygia & Pisidia. Proinde Synodus quae convenit apud Laodiceam Phrygiae, lege prohibuit ne precarentur Angelos. Et in hodiernum usque diem oratoria Sancti Michaelis apud illos illorumque finitimos videre est. Illi ergo humilitate nimirum ducti hoc fieri suadebant, dicentes universorum Deum nec cerni, nec attingi, nec comprehendi posse; & oportere per Angelos divinam sibi benevolentiam conciliare.
latin.1644: LXXXVII. Igitur ex mente Patrum Synodi Laodicenae & Theodoreti Canonem illius exponentis, Angelos nominare, & Angelos precari, ut per eos divinam benevolentiam nobis conciliemus, est cultum illicitum Angelis exhibere, & peccare contra praeceptum Apostoli damnantis Angelorum culturam & Religionem. Et ad veterum haereticorum morem, non ad usum Ecclesiae Orthodoxae pertinet, Oratoria Angelis, & ipsi Sancto Michaeli struere: quod quam belle congruat cum hodierna praxi Ecclesiae Romanae judicandum omnibus relinquo. Siquidem illa, ut fatetur & observat Dionysius Petavius Jesuita, Angelorum praesidium & patrocinium precibus & votis ambit, eosque Mediatores ad Deum allegat; tum oratoria & basilicas in illorum honorem excitat, ac festos dies & hilares eorum dicat cultui. Theol. dogm. lib. 2. cap. 9. num. 13.
latin.1645: LXXXVIII. Nam ita absurdum est, ut non egeat refutatione, quod observat Estius; nempe Theodoretum per Oratoria Sancto Michaeli dicata, non intelligere loca ab haereticis consecrata illicito suo Angelorum cultui; sed quae ante haereticorum idololatria polluta, tum temporis Episcoporum Catholicorum prudentia in Oratoria Sancti Michaelis conversa erant. Nam insanum oportet fingere Theodoretum, ut dicat quod pertendit Estius, haereticos veteres solitos Angelos precari, id vero prohibuisse Synodum Laodicenam, & propterea loco ubi Angelos precabantur, Orthodoxorum prudenti concilio, fuisse in Oratoria Sancti Michaelis mutata. Adde quod de ista locorum conversione & mutatione deque praesumpta illa Episcoporum prudentia ne hilum quidem apud Theodoretum innuitur. Legentibus vero etiam invitis, sese obtrudit Theodoreti Scopus, qui est probare quod dixerat, hoc vitium eorum qui Angelos invocabant perdiu in Phrygia & Pisidia mansisse, ex eo quod ad tempora usque Theodoreti ipsius, visebantur apud Phrygas, & finitimos eorum Pisidas, Oratoria ab ipsis Michaeli dicata. Qualia Oratoria in reliquis orbis Christiani partibus non reperiebantur. Commentar. in epist. ad Col. cap. 2.
latin.1646: LXXXIX. Caeterum nec Angelos, nec Beatos justorum Spiritus precandos & invocandos esse ex eo constat, quod Scriptura sacra Orationem & invocationem pro insigni cultus divini parte habet, & eximio atque praecipuo nostrae Religionis erga Deum officio. Unde est quod templum Dei in Scriptura dicitur Domus Orationis; & fidelium preces atque orationes ut spirituale quoddam sacrificium proponuntur; & eum solum docemur invocare in quem fides nostra recumbit. Juxta illud Apostoli Quomodo invocabunt in quem non crediderunt? Es. 56. 7. Matth. 21. 13. Psal. 141. 2. Heb. 13. 15. Rom. 10. 14.
latin.1647: XC. Respondent Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae Orationem illam quam Scriptura proponit, ut partem cultus qui Deo proprius est, esse orationem absolutam, qua rogatur aliquis, ut ipse bonorum author atque largitor; non autem relativam, qua rogamus aliquem ut Deum pro nobis oret, & ea quibus egemus nobis a Deo impetret: se vero Angelos & Sanctos invocare non ut ipsos bonorum authores; sed solum ut eorundem bonorum impetratores, & nostros apud Deum intercessores: adeoque se non aliud ab Angelis & Sanctis petere quam ut Deum pro nobis orent: quemadmodum absque ulla in Deum injuria, rogamus ipsos fideles nobiscum in terra viventes, ut nos apud Deum precibus suis juvent.
latin.1648: XCI. Sed Ecclesia Romana, dum Angelos & Sanctos invocat, non simpliciter dicit illis Orate pro nobis, nec solum ab eis petit ut apud Deum pro nobis intercedant, sed pluribus apud eos orationibus utitur ejusdem omnino formae cum iis quas ad Deum concipere solemus. Idque non tantum in privata fidelium devotione, sed in publico & solenni cultu: in quo Beatae Virgini dicitur Tu nos ab hoste Protege, Et Hora mortis suscipe. Vitam praesta puram, Iter para tutum. Nos culpis solutos, mites fac & castos. Et Joanni Baptistae, Nos miserando respice, Culpasque nostras ablue. Joanni autem Apostolo Tolle pestem, aufer ulcus, & foveto languidos: Pelle morbum caede hostem, & remove scandalum. Quibus similia multa aliis quoque Sanctis dici solent. Ut in priori harum thesium parte a nobis fuse ostensum est.
latin.1649: XCII. Regerunt, quum Sanctos eo modo precantur, mentem suam non esse, ut Sancti ea bona praestent & largiantur ipsi, propria quadam potestate, sed solum ut illa meritis & precibus suis a Deo obtineant. Adeoque licet verba aliud sonent, se tamen aliud non intelligere, quam ut Sancti intercessione sua quae petunt a Deo impetrent. Sed certe nihil eos cogit ut aliter sentiant, & aliter loquantur. Si non aliud rogant Sanctos quam ut Deum pro ipsis orent, cur utuntur apud ipsos verbis orationis absolutae; nec contenti sunt Sanctis ingeminare illud solenne, Ora pro nobis?
latin.1650: XCIII. Certe Sanctos hic nobiscum viventes omnium confessione rogare licet ut Deum pro nobis orent: Nec tamen ferretur qui viro Sancto in terris versanti diceret, ut Mariae Virgini dici solet, Nostra tolle Incommoda, Dona confer caelestia. Nos culpis solutos, Mites fac & castos. Aut ut dicitur S. Benedicto Angustum per iter scandere largiens Dona regna perennia. Sive ut habet hymnus ad Sanctum Nicolaum Aufer mortis dispendia, Confer vitae subsidia: Ut post carnis exilia, Tecum simus in gloria. Quod si quis Apostolos ipsos ea ratione fuisset allocutus, Orationem ejusmodi ut impiam compescuissent, & jussissent ista non a se, sed a Domino peti. An ergo putabimus jam ipsis gratum esse posse, quod olim dum in terris viverent, ut impium & sacrilegum aversati fuissent?
latin.1651: XCIV. Adde quod in usu Ecclesiae Romanae non paucae preces ad Sanctos directae reperiuntur, in quibus ab ipsis non solum postulantur bona Gratiae & Gloriae, sed etiam rogantur ut ea nobis praestent tradita sibi potestate, & jussu ac praecepto suo. Quod plane aliud est quam ejusmodi bona suis orationibus nobis a Deo impetrare. Veluti quum Apostolis in communi dicitur, Qui caelum verbo clauditis, Serasque ejus solvitis, Nos a peccatis omnibus, Solvite jussu quaesumus. Quorum praecepto subditur, Salus & languor omnium, Sanate aegros moribus, Nos reddentes virtutibus. Item, Nos a reatu noxios, Solvi jubete quaesumus. Et speciatim ad Petrum Apostolum, Peccati vincula Resolve tibi potestate tradita, Qua cunctis caelum Verbo claudis, aperis. Ut supra quoque fusius a nobis probatum est.
latin.1652: XCV. Etiamsi vero Ecclesia Romana non aliud a Sanctis petere quam ut Deum pro nobis orent, istud tamen ut legitimum minime defendi posset exemplo precum illarum quas fideles a se invicem postulant; dum scilicet, aliqua necessitate pressi, fratres suos rogant ut ipsos apud Deum orationum suarum auxilio juvare velint. Nam ex eo quod in Scriptura monemur & fratres nostros precibus adjuvare, & mutuum ejusmodi auxilium ab ipsis petere, non sequitur aliquem in Europa degentem posse absque stultitia, aut etiam impietate, ore vel corde compellare virum Sanctum commorantem apud Sinas aut Americanos, eumque quasi videntem & audientem rogare, ut apud Deum pro ipso intercedat, & quae sentit sibi opus esse impetret. Quomodo ergo inde concludemus nos posse pie & cum ratione, a Sanctis in Christo defunctis postulare, seu voce, seu etiam solo cordis affectu, ut Deum pro nobis precentur; cum illi jam in caelestem paradisum evecti, tantum a nobis absint, quantum summum a terra caelum; nec ullum, donec simili beatitudine fruamur, supersit nobis cum ipsis commercium; & ratio mutuos conceptus communicandi? Itaque ex precibus quas a se mutuo postulant fideles in terra simul Militantes, non magis sequitur Sanctos in caelum jam receptos a nobis invocari posse, quam olim sequebatur, secundum doctrinam Ecclesiae Romanae, animas patrum in Limbo detentas a fidelibus tum temporis viventibus fuisse invocandas.
latin.1653: XCVI. Supponunt quidem Scholae Romanae Theologi Spiritus justorum in caelum admissos non obstante tanta locorum distantia, ea scire atque percipere quae in terris geruntur; & Sanctorum singulos posse simul omnium hominum ipsos invocantium, non solum preces audire, & necessitates videre, sed & intimas cogitationes & arcanos cordis affectus intueri, & certo novisse. Verum hoc absque Dei verbo, & certa ratione supponi non debuit: istudque ex conjecturis & suspicionibus nostris pronunciare, plane est pedem inferre in ea quae non vidimus.
latin.1654: XCVII. Neque nostrum est contrarium probare; quamvis multa in hanc rem ex Scriptura afferri possent. Nam ut ab implorandis Sanctorum defunctorum precibus atque suffragiis abstinere debeamus, sufficit ut nesciamus an ipsi nos audiant; nec videamus istud in Dei Verbo revelatum. Affirmantibus vero rem ita se habere probandum incumbit quod dicunt; & quam Sanctorum animabus tribuunt rerum nostrarum notitiam, invicto argumento, aut claro aliquo Scripturae oraculo demonstrare tenentur. Alioquin ista ipsorum erga pias Sanctorum animas devotio prorsus nutabit, & absque fide fiet.
latin.1655: XCVIII. Quam autem infirma atque levia sint quae ad tantae rei fidem faciendam ex Scriptura proferunt, excutienti facile apparebit. Primum igitur Sanctos in caelis cum Christo regnantes nosse quae in terris geruntur, ac proinde percipere preces omnium qui illos invocant, & eorum cogitationes ac corda intueri, ex eo probant quod nonnulli viventes absentia & futura; adeoque cordis occulta non ignorarunt. Ut, exempli causa, Helisaeus, qui dicebat servo suo Giezi, Nonne Cor meum in praesenti erat, quando descendit homo de curru suo in occursum tuum? Et Samuel qui Sauli inquiebat, Omnia quae sunt in corde tuo dicam tibi; & de asinis Patris tui, quos perdidisti. Et sic Petrus absens sciebat Ananiam & Sapphiram fraudasse de pretio agri. Et Paulus intuitus cor claudi mendici, cognovit eum fidem habere, ut salvus fieret. Sed cujusmodi est ista consequentia, Prophetae atque Apostoli occulta quaedam, quae ad munus ipsorum pertinebant, Deo revelante, noverunt: ergo Beatorum animae, in gloriam caelestem receptae, norunt ea quae in terris geruntur, ac omnium qui eos invocant necessitates vident, ac preces percipiunt, sive ore, sive solo corde & affectu conceptas? Inde quidem sequitur Deum posse quas libuerit hominum hic viventium necessitates, actiones, & cogitationes Beatis Spiritibus justorum revelare; sed an istud faciat, vel non, inde concludi nullo modo potest. 2. Reg. 5. 1 Sam. 9. Act. 5. Act. 14.
latin.1656: XCIX. Quod si quis dicat officium Sanctis defunctis a Deo demandatum exigere ut rerum nostrarum notitiam habeant, quia scilicet, Patroni & intercessores nostri a Deo constituti sunt, ignotum probat per aeque ignotum. Nec enim Dei verbum ullibi docet Sanctos gloria caelesti fruentes a Deo nobis datos esse praesides & Mediatores, qui apud Deum pro nobis intercedant: imo contrarium satis evidenter ex Scriptura sacra colligitur. Nec etiam dici potest ad beatitudinem Sanctorum pertinere, ut audiant ipsos invocantium preces, quia nimirum hoc facit ad majorem eorum gloriam. Nam si Sanctorum in Christo defunctorum invocatio res superstitiosa atque illicita est, & ab hominibus tantum excogitata, ad gloriam Sanctorum nullo modo pertinet ut norint qui ipsos invocent: & prius probatum oportuit, Deo gratum & acceptum esse ut Sancti cum ipso regnantes invocentur, quam ut cum aliqua probabilitatis specie supponatur ejusmodi invocationem ad gloriam eorum facere.
latin.1657: C. Praeterea Sanctos in caelo triumphantes non ignorare quae homines agunt, & quae iis accidunt in hoc mundo inferiori; imo ab iis occultas non esse hominum cogitationes, inde probant Scholae Romanae Theologi, quod ista cognitionem Angelorum non effugiunt. Christus enim ipse testatur justos in caelis fore ἰσαγγέλους sicut Angelos Dei; apud Matthaeum capite vigesimo secundo. Ac proinde cum debeant Angelis aequales esse, non putandum est illos ab Angelis notitia rerum nostrarum superari. Jam vero caelestibus Angelis nota esse quae in terris aguntur, adeoque ipsos cordium humanorum interiores motus atque affectus, ex eo sequi existimant quod dicuntur gaudere super uno peccatore poenitentiam agente, magis quam super nonaginta novem justis. Si enim peccatorum poenitentia ipsis perspecta est, utique norunt quid in mundo agatur; non modo foris, sed intus etiam in corde peccatoris, in quo est vera poenitentia & dolor de Peccatis. Luc. 15. 10.
latin.1658: CI. Sed mirum non est Angelos qui sunt spiritus administratorii in ministerium missi propter eos qui haereditatem capient salutis, cum ex officio nobis adsint, & circa nos versentur, ea scire quae ad nos attinent, & in primis peccatorum poenitentiam & conversionem, cui procurandae ex Dei mandato inserviunt: sed ut jam diximus, munus simile beatis justorum animabus a Deo demandatum esse, ex Dei verbo ostendi non potest. Neque huc facit quod affirmat Christus justos in caelo fore ἰσαγγέλους. Haec enim cum Angelis aequalitas seu similitudo extendi non debet ultra Christi scopum; qui est docere justos post resurrectionem vitam ducturos Angelicam, quatenus hujus vitae necessitatibus & infirmitatibus non amplius subjacebunt, & neque uxorem ducent, neque nuptui dabuntur, ut legenti verba Christi apud Matthaeum planum est. Adde, quod non sequitur, singulos Angelos singulorum hominum cogitationes nosse, & vota percipere, ex eo quod Christus indefinite dicit Angelis gaudium esse propter conversionem unius peccatoris. Sicut vere dicere possumus in Ecclesia Dei gaudium magnum esse, quum peccator unus ad Deum convertitur; Nec tamen inde sequitur singulis qui in Ecclesia sunt, aliorum omnium cogitata, dicta & facta nota esse. Heb. 1. 13.

sections.title: Perron's evasion: the 'religion of angels' as the law given through angels
sections.pass_a: To this the Doctors of the Roman Church answer and devise various things; but their emptiness would at once appear to one weighing and considering the matter without passion and prejudice. Cardinal Perron does not want to be understood by the Religion of Angels that by which the Angels are worshipped, but rather that which was handed down by the Angels; and he conjectures that by that name the Jewish religion, or the Mosaic rites, is designated, since in other places the law is said by Paul to be Ordained through Angels in the hand of a Mediator. And therefore in his mind the Scope of the Apostle is to call the Colossians back from Jewish worship and from the ceremonies of the Mosaic law. Against the King of Great Britain, book 5, chapter 6. Galatians 3.
pass_b: The teachers of the Roman Church give various answers to this and invent various shifts, but anyone who weighs the matter without partisanship or prejudice will see at once how empty they are.

Cardinal Perron will not have "the religion of angels" mean the religion by which angels are worshiped. He takes it rather to mean the religion handed down by angels, and he guesses that the name stands for the Jewish religion, that is, the rites of Moses, because elsewhere Paul says the law was "ordained through angels in the hand of a mediator" (Galatians 3:19). On his reading, then, the Apostle's aim is to call the Colossians back from Jewish worship and the ceremonies of the law of Moses. (Perron, Reply to the King of Great Britain, book 5, chapter 6.)

choices.term: eam quae ab Angelis tradita est
choices.english: the religion handed down by angels
choices.why: Perron's point turns on reading the genitive as source rather than object; the English keeps the contrast with 'by which angels are worshiped' explicit.

notes: The 1675 margin gives only Gal. 3; the words cited are Galatians 3:19, so the English gives 3:19.
Perron's work is his Réplique à la réponse du sérénissime roi de la Grande-Bretagne (1620); the margin cites book 5, chapter 6.

sections.title: Perron's reading is new: the Fathers and Rome's own interpreters read it as worship of angels
sections.pass_a: But first that comment of Perron is plainly new, and unheard of among all Christians up to his times. For not only the ancients, as Origen, Chrysostom, Hilary under the name of Ambrose, Pelagius under the name of Jerome, Theodoret, Theophylact and Oecumenius, understand by the Religion of Angels that of which Angels would be the object; but not even any one of the interpreters of the Roman Church before him took the words of Paul in the sense in which Perron did. Nor even could the authority of so great a Cardinal make that comment acceptable to the most learned men in that Church after him. But it was expressly rejected by them as empty, as among others by Petavius the Jesuit, a Noble Antiquary. Theological Dogmas, Tome 3, book 2, chapter 9, paragraph 16.
pass_b: First, this invention of Perron's is plainly new; no Christian had heard of it before his time.

The ancients, such as Origen, Chrysostom, Hilary writing under Ambrose's name, Pelagius writing under Jerome's name, Theodoret, Theophylact and Oecumenius, all take "the religion of angels" to mean a religion with angels as its object. And not one interpreter of the Roman Church before Perron took Paul's words in Perron's sense.

Nor could even so great a cardinal's authority win that invention over the most learned men of his own church after him. They rejected it outright as empty, among them the Jesuit Petavius, a distinguished student of antiquity (Theological Dogmas, tome 3, book 2, chapter 9, paragraph 16).

lemmas.gloss: Hilary under Ambrose's name (the commentator now called Ambrosiaster)

choices.english: a distinguished student of antiquity
choices.why: Le Blanc praises Petavius' learning in early Christian sources; 'antiquary' alone would read as a collector of objects.

notes: Hilarius sub Ambrosii nomine is the Latin commentator on Paul now called Ambrosiaster; Pelagius sub Hieronymi nomine is Pelagius' Pauline commentary transmitted under Jerome's name.

sections.title: The law of Moses is never called 'religion of angels', and Colossians 2:16-18 forbids the reading
sections.pass_a: And certainly not only is the Mosaic law nowhere in sacred Scripture called the threskeia, the Religion, of Angels, but not even any example of this nomenclature can be found among any authors whatever, whether profane or Ecclesiastical. Nor, if such a naming were usual, could it be fitted to that place of Paul. For since Paul in what precedes had abundantly fortified the Colossians in clear and express words against the fraud of Judaizing impostors, saying Let no one judge you in food, or in drink, or in respect of a feast day, or of the New Moon, or of the Sabbaths; which are a shadow of things to come, but the body is of Christ; what did it matter to repeat the same thing in those obscure and ambiguous words? Add that Paul affirms that those introducers of the religion of Angels walk in the things which they have not seen, that is, set foot into the things which they do not know, and chatter about unknown things: which indeed fits best the worshippers of Angels, who blurt out many unascertained things about the nature, orders and offices of Angels: but does not suit those devoted to the Mosaic law; since the Mosaic discipline was accurately explained in the sacred volumes, and set out for all who wished to know it.
pass_b: Certainly Scripture nowhere calls the law of Moses "the religion (threskeia) of angels." No author of any kind, secular or churchly, can be found who uses that name for it.

And even if the name were common, it could not fit this passage of Paul. In the verses just before, Paul had already armed the Colossians in plain, explicit words against the deceit of the Judaizing impostors: "Let no one judge you in food or in drink, or in respect of a feast day, or of the new moon, or of the sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come, but the body is of Christ" (Colossians 2:16-17). What point would there be in repeating the same thing in those dark and ambiguous words?

Paul also says that those who brought in the religion of angels walk in things they have not seen (Colossians 2:18): that is, they set foot in what they do not know and chatter about the unknown. That fits the worshipers of angels very well, for they pour out a great many unverified claims about the nature, orders and duties of angels. It does not fit men devoted to the law of Moses, since the discipline of Moses had been set out precisely in the sacred books and laid open to anyone who wished to learn it.

choices.term: pedem inferre in ea quae non norunt
choices.english: set foot in what they do not know
choices.why: Le Blanc's gloss on embateuon is spatial; the English keeps the image of trespass.

notes: The 1675 print gives no margin here; the quoted words are Colossians 2:16-17 and the phrase 'walk in what they have not seen' is Colossians 2:18, supplied in the English.

sections.title: Rome's second evasion, that Paul condemns only false angel-worship, fails: he forbids it outright
sections.pass_a: Therefore the Theologians of the Roman School run back to another place, that they may defend the faith and practice of their Church against so express a law of the Apostle. And to this returns the solution of most and of the more Learned, that the Apostle does not condemn the religious worship and invocation of Angels, or of Saints; but only false, superstitious and idolatrous worship and adoration. Such as they say Simon Magus, and Cerinthus, and the Disciples of both taught. But that is their mere fiction, which has no foundation in the words and doctrine of the Apostle. For the Apostle in no way teaches or hints that there is some threskeia of Angels, or religion, pious and lawful, and that he condemns only that which is immoderate and idolatrous. But simply and in general he condemns the religion of Angels. Therefore whatever the errors of the ancient heretics were about the nature, offices and worship of Angels, that does not hinder those also from violating Paul's prohibition who today pursue Angels with religious worship, and show any threskeia whatever to Angels and Saints; since the Apostle absolutely prohibits the threskeia of Angels; not only that which Simon or Cerinthus are said to have given them. And it is manifest that they perform threskeia to Angels and Saints who worship them with vows, prayers, hymns, basilicas, oratories, feasts, gifts, and offerings of every kind, as is customary in the Roman Church: and consequently that what the Roman Church does in this part is condemned by the Apostle, no less than what Simon, or Cerinthus, or any similar heretics there were, are reported to have done.
pass_b: So the theologians of the Roman school fall back on another defense to protect their church's belief and practice against so explicit a law of the Apostle. The answer of most of them, and of the more learned, comes to this: the Apostle does not condemn the religious worship and invocation of angels or of saints, but only a false, superstitious and idolatrous worship and adoration, such as they say Simon Magus and Cerinthus and the followers of each taught.

But that is pure invention on their part, with no footing in the Apostle's words or teaching. Nowhere does he teach or so much as hint that there is a pious and lawful religion (threskeia) of angels and that he condemns only the excessive and idolatrous kind. He condemns the religion of angels plainly and as a whole.

So whatever errors the old heretics held about the nature, duties and worship of angels, that does not stop people today from breaking Paul's prohibition when they pursue angels with religious worship and offer any kind of threskeia to angels and saints. The Apostle forbids the threskeia of angels absolutely, not merely the kind Simon or Cerinthus are said to have offered them.

It is plain that those who worship angels and saints with vows, prayers, hymns, basilicas, oratories, feasts, gifts and offerings of every kind, as is the established custom in the Roman Church, do offer them threskeia. It follows that what the Roman Church does here is condemned by the Apostle no less than what Simon or Cerinthus, or any heretics like them, are reported to have done.

choices.english: plainly and as a whole
choices.why: The argument is that Paul's prohibition has no qualifier; the English stresses that it is unrestricted.

sections.title: Rome's third reply: worship of ministers is not divine. But the Colossian errorists also took angels for ministers
sections.pass_a: The Doctors of the Roman School reply that by whatever rites and acts Angels and Saints are worshipped among them, that worship is not divine: since they worship Angels and Saints not as Gods, but as Ministers of God, and our intercessors with God: but that threskeia or Religion is the worship proper to God, and which is shown to someone as God. But from the very text of the Apostle it can be sufficiently gathered that those whom he there rebukes, and against whom he teaches that one must beware, did not hold Angels for Gods, but for messengers and Ministers of the highest God, and our Mediators and intercessors with God, which the very name of Angels which they attributed to them proves: for Angel signifies messenger. Add that those seducers professed themselves Christians, and worshipped Angels under the pretext of humility, as if they were unworthy to approach God immediately, and therefore had need with him of the mediation and intercession of Angels. Whence it is sufficiently clear that they worshipped Angels with a certain subaltern worship, below that which they thought was owed to the highest God: And so, according to the mind of the Apostle, those also give threskeia to Angels who worship Angels with a certain inferior worship, and do not hold Angels for Gods.
pass_b: The teachers of the Roman school answer that whatever rites and acts they use in worshiping angels and saints, that worship is not divine. They worship angels and saints, they say, not as gods but as God's servants and our intercessors with God, whereas threskeia, or religion, is the worship that belongs to God and is given to someone as God.

But the Apostle's own text shows well enough that the people he rebukes there, and warns us against, did not take angels for gods. They took them for messengers and servants of the supreme God, and for our mediators and advocates with God. The very name they gave them shows this, since "angel" means messenger.

Besides, those seducers professed to be Christians, and they worshiped angels on the pretext of humility, as if they were unworthy to come to God directly and so needed the mediation and intercession of angels with him. So it is clear enough that they worshiped angels with a subordinate worship, lower than the worship they thought due to the supreme God. On the Apostle's meaning, then, people who worship angels with a lower worship, without taking them for gods, are still giving angels threskeia.

lemmas.gloss: with a subordinate kind of worship

choices.english: mediators and advocates
choices.why: Deprecator here is one who pleads for another, not one who averts or deprecates.

sections.title: The Angelici and Laodicea: Theodoret on praying to angels in Phrygia and Pisidia
sections.pass_a: But what the Religion toward Angels of those pseudo-Christians was, who by the ancients were called Angelici, we can gather from the Synod of Laodicea: of which this Canon is found inserted in the Code of Canons of the Universal Church. That Christians ought not to leave the Church of God, and go away, and name Angels, and make Congregations, which is forbidden. But what it is, in the mind of that council, to name Angels, Theodoret explains, writing on the Epistle to the Colossians, and expounding that place which we press. Those who defended the law, he says, led them also to worship Angels, saying that the law had been given through them: And this vice remained a very long time in Phrygia and Pisidia. Therefore the Synod which met at Laodicea of Phrygia prohibited by law that they pray to Angels. And to this present day oratories of Saint Michael are to be seen among them and their neighbors. They therefore, led namely by humility, urged that this be done, saying that the God of all things can neither be seen, nor touched, nor comprehended; and that it is fitting to win the divine goodwill for themselves through Angels.
pass_b: What kind of religion toward angels those false Christians had, whom the ancients called Angelici, we can learn from the Synod of Laodicea. One of its canons was taken into the Code of Canons of the Universal Church: "Christians ought not to forsake the Church of God and go off to name angels and hold assemblies, which is forbidden."

What "naming angels" meant to that council Theodoret explains in his commentary on the Epistle to the Colossians, on the very passage we are pressing. "Those who defended the law," he says, "also led people to worship angels, saying that the law had been given through them. This vice lasted a long time in Phrygia and Pisidia. That is why the synod that met at Laodicea in Phrygia forbade by law that anyone pray to angels. And to this day one can see oratories of Saint Michael among them and their neighbors. They urged this practice out of humility, as they claimed, saying that the God of all things cannot be seen or reached or grasped, and that we ought to win God's goodwill for ourselves through angels."

lemmas.gloss: the 'Angelics', a sect named for angel-worship

choices.english: out of humility, as they claimed
choices.why: Nimirum here is ironic; the English marks the humility as their own pretext.

notes: The canon is Laodicea canon 35; the quotation from Theodoret is his commentary on Colossians 2:18.

sections.title: So Laodicea and Theodoret condemn naming and praying to angels, and Petavius admits Rome does both
sections.pass_a: Therefore in the mind of the Fathers of the Synod of Laodicea and of Theodoret expounding its Canon, to name Angels, and to pray to Angels, that through them we may win the divine goodwill for ourselves, is to show unlawful worship to Angels, and to sin against the precept of the Apostle condemning the cultivation and Religion of Angels. And it belongs to the custom of the ancient heretics, not to the usage of the Orthodox Church, to build Oratories to Angels, and to Saint Michael himself: how nicely this agrees with the present practice of the Roman Church I leave to all to judge. Since that Church, as Dionysius Petavius the Jesuit confesses and observes, seeks the protection and patronage of Angels with prayers and vows, and alleges them as Mediators to God; then raises oratories and basilicas in their honor, and dedicates feast days and joyful ones to their worship. Theological Dogmas, book 2, chapter 9, number 13.
pass_b: So in the judgment of the fathers of the Synod of Laodicea, and of Theodoret who expounds their canon, to name angels and pray to angels in order to win God's goodwill through them is to give angels unlawful worship and to sin against the Apostle's command, which condemns the cult and religion of angels.

Building oratories to angels, and to Saint Michael himself, belongs to the custom of the old heretics, not to the practice of the orthodox Church. How well that fits the present practice of the Roman Church I leave everyone to judge. For that church, as the Jesuit Dionysius Petavius admits and observes, "seeks the protection and patronage of angels with prayers and vows, and puts them forward as mediators with God; it also raises oratories and basilicas in their honor, and dedicates festal and joyful days to their worship" (Theological Dogmas, book 2, chapter 9, number 13).

choices.english: how well that fits
choices.why: Belle is ironic; the English keeps the understatement rather than spelling out the charge.

sections.title: Estius' claim that the Michael oratories were converted pagan shrines has no basis in Theodoret
sections.pass_a: For so absurd is it, that it does not need refutation, what Estius observes; namely that Theodoret by the Oratories dedicated to Saint Michael does not understand places consecrated by heretics to their unlawful worship of Angels; but those which, polluted before by the idolatry of heretics, had then by the prudence of Catholic Bishops been converted into Oratories of Saint Michael. For one must feign Theodoret insane, so that he says what Estius contends, that the ancient heretics were accustomed to pray to Angels, that the Synod of Laodicea forbade this, and that therefore the place where they prayed to Angels had, by the prudent counsel of the Orthodox, been changed into Oratories of Saint Michael. Add that about that conversion and change of places and about that presumed prudence of the Bishops not a whit is hinted in Theodoret. But to readers, even unwilling, Theodoret's Scope forces itself, which is to prove what he had said, that this vice of those who invoked Angels remained a very long time in Phrygia and Pisidia, from the fact that up to the times of Theodoret himself, Oratories dedicated by them to Michael were seen among the Phrygians, and their neighbors the Pisidians. Such Oratories were not found in the remaining parts of the Christian world. Commentary on the Epistle to the Colossians, chapter 2.
pass_b: Estius' remark is so absurd that it needs no refutation. He says that by the oratories dedicated to Saint Michael Theodoret does not mean places the heretics consecrated to their unlawful worship of angels, but places once defiled by the heretics' idolatry and later turned into oratories of Saint Michael by the prudence of the catholic bishops.

One would have to imagine Theodoret out of his mind to have him say what Estius maintains: that the old heretics used to pray to angels, the Synod of Laodicea forbade it, and therefore the place where they prayed to angels was changed into oratories of Saint Michael by the wise counsel of the orthodox. Besides, Theodoret does not hint at any such conversion of places, or at any such supposed prudence of bishops.

Theodoret's purpose forces itself even on unwilling readers. He means to prove what he had said, that the vice of those who called on angels lasted a long time in Phrygia and Pisidia, from the fact that down to his own day oratories dedicated by them to Michael could be seen among the Phrygians and their neighbors the Pisidians. No such oratories were found in the rest of the Christian world (Theodoret, Commentary on the Epistle to the Colossians, chapter 2).

choices.english: one would have to imagine Theodoret out of his mind
choices.why: Le Blanc's point is that Estius' reading makes Theodoret's argument incoherent.

notes: Estius is Willem Hessels van Est (Guilielmus Estius, d. 1613), Catholic commentator on the Pauline epistles.

sections.title: Prayer is a chief part of divine worship, so angels and saints are not to be invoked
sections.pass_a: But moreover that neither Angels, nor the Blessed Spirits of the just, are to be prayed to and invoked is established from this, that sacred Scripture holds Prayer and invocation for a notable part of divine worship, and for a special and principal duty of our Religion toward God. Whence it is that the temple of God is called in Scripture the House of Prayer; and the prayers and petitions of the faithful are set forth as a certain spiritual sacrifice; and we are taught to invoke him alone on whom our faith rests. According to that of the Apostle How shall they invoke him in whom they have not believed? Isaiah 56:7. Matthew 21:13. Psalm 141:2. Hebrews 13:15. Romans 10:14.
pass_b: That neither angels nor the blessed spirits of the just are to be prayed to or invoked is settled by this: Scripture counts prayer and invocation a principal part of divine worship and a chief and special duty of our religion toward God.

That is why Scripture calls God's temple "the house of prayer" (Isaiah 56:7; Matthew 21:13), and sets the prayers and supplications of the faithful before us as a kind of spiritual sacrifice (Psalm 141:2; Hebrews 13:15). And we are taught to call only on him in whom our faith rests, as the Apostle says: "How shall they call on him in whom they have not believed?" (Romans 10:14).

lemmas.gloss: as a notable part of divine worship

choices.english: in whom our faith rests
choices.why: Recumbit is the language of reliance; 'rests' keeps it without adding a doctrine.

sections.title: Rome's distinction: absolute prayer to God, relative prayer to the saints as intercessors
sections.pass_a: The Doctors of the Roman Church answer that the Prayer which Scripture sets forth as part of the worship which is proper to God is absolute prayer, by which someone is asked as himself the author and giver of goods; not however relative, by which we ask someone that he pray to God for us, and obtain for us from God the things we need: but that they invoke Angels and Saints not as themselves authors of goods; but only as obtainers of those same goods, and our intercessors with God: and so they ask nothing else of Angels and Saints than that they pray to God for us: just as, without any injury to God, we ask the faithful themselves living with us on earth to help us with God by their prayers.
pass_b: The teachers of the Roman Church reply that the prayer Scripture sets forth as part of the worship proper to God is absolute prayer, by which someone is asked as himself the author and giver of good things. It is not relative prayer, by which we ask someone to pray to God for us and obtain from God what we need.

They say they call on angels and saints not as authors of good things but only as those who obtain them for us, our intercessors with God. So they ask nothing more of angels and saints than that they pray to God for us, just as, without any wrong to God, we ask our fellow believers who live with us on earth to help us before God with their prayers.

lemmas.gloss: obtainers, those who secure by asking

choices.english: relative prayer
choices.why: The scholastic term is kept and explained in the same sentence.

sections.title: But Rome's public hymns ask the saints directly for what only God gives
sections.pass_a: But the Roman Church, while it invokes Angels and Saints, does not simply say to them Pray for us, nor only ask of them that they intercede for us with God, but uses with them many prayers of altogether the same form as those which we are accustomed to compose to God. And that not only in the private devotion of the faithful, but in public and solemn worship: in which it is said to the Blessed Virgin Protect us from the enemy, And receive us in the hour of death. Grant a pure life, Prepare a safe way. Make us, loosed from faults, gentle and chaste. And to John the Baptist, Look upon us with pity, And wash away our faults. But to John the Apostle Take away the plague, remove the sore, and cherish the languid: Drive out disease, slay the enemy, and remove the stumbling block. Similar to which many things are wont to be said to other Saints also. As was shown at length by us in the former part of these theses.
pass_b: But when the Roman Church calls on angels and saints, it does not simply say to them, "Pray for us," or ask only that they intercede for us with God. It addresses them in many prayers of exactly the same form as those we are used to making to God.

It does this not only in the private devotion of the faithful but in public, solemn worship. To the Blessed Virgin it says: "Protect us from the enemy, and receive us at the hour of death. Grant us a pure life, prepare us a safe road. Make us free of our faults, gentle and chaste." To John the Baptist: "Look on us with pity, and wash away our faults." And to John the Apostle: "Take away the plague, remove the sore, and tend the sick; drive out disease, strike down the enemy, and take away the stumbling block."
Many like things are said to other saints too, as we showed at length in the first part of these theses.

choices.term: Nos culpis solutos, mites fac & castos
choices.english: Make us free of our faults, gentle and chaste
choices.why: These are lines of the hymn Ave maris stella; the English keeps them as direct petitions.
rejected: Loose us from guilt and make us mild
Absolve us and make us chaste

notes: The first two lines to the Virgin are the Maria mater gratiae doxology; the next lines are from Ave maris stella.

sections.title: Rome's retort that the words mean only intercession: then why use the words of absolute prayer?
sections.pass_a: They retort that, when they pray to the Saints in that way, their mind is not that the Saints themselves furnish and bestow those goods, by some power of their own, but only that they obtain them from God by their merits and prayers. And so although the words sound otherwise, they nevertheless understand nothing else than that the Saints obtain from God by their intercession what they ask. But certainly nothing compels them to think one thing and say another. If they ask nothing else of the Saints than that they pray to God for them, why do they use with them the words of absolute prayer; and are not content to repeat to the Saints that solemn Pray for us?
pass_b: They retort that when they pray to the saints in that way, they do not mean that the saints give and bestow those good things themselves by any power of their own, but only that the saints obtain them from God by their merits and prayers. So, although the words say something else, all they mean is that the saints obtain from God by intercession what is asked.

But surely nothing forces them to think one thing and say another. If they ask the saints only to pray to God for them, why do they address the saints in the words of absolute prayer? Why are they not content to repeat to the saints the familiar "Pray for us"?

lemmas.gloss: by some power of their own

choices.english: to think one thing and say another
choices.why: Keeps Le Blanc's balanced antithesis.
rejected: to feel otherwise and speak otherwise

sections.title: We may ask living saints to pray for us, but no one would address them as Rome addresses Mary, Benedict or Nicholas
sections.pass_a: Certainly by everyone's confession it is lawful to ask Saints living here with us that they pray to God for us: Yet he would not be tolerated who would say to a holy man living on earth, as is wont to be said to the Virgin Mary, Take away our Ills, Bestow heavenly gifts. Make us, loosed from faults, Gentle and chaste. Or as is said to Saint Benedict Granting to climb by the narrow way, Give the everlasting kingdoms. Or as the hymn to Saint Nicholas has it Take away the losses of death, Bestow the helps of life: That after the exile of the flesh, We may be with thee in glory. But if anyone had addressed the Apostles themselves in that manner, they would have checked such a Prayer as impious, and ordered that those things be asked not from them, but from the Lord. Shall we then think that this can now be pleasing to them, which formerly while they lived on earth they would have shunned as impious and sacrilegious?
pass_b: Everyone admits it is lawful to ask holy people living here with us to pray to God for us. Yet no one would be tolerated who said to a holy man on earth what is commonly said to the Virgin Mary: "Take away our ills, bestow heavenly gifts; make us free of our faults, gentle and chaste." Or what is said to Saint Benedict: "You who grant us to climb the narrow road, give us the everlasting kingdom." Or what the hymn to Saint Nicholas says: "Take away the loss that death brings, bestow the helps of life, so that after the exile of the flesh we may be with you in glory."

If anyone had spoken that way to the apostles themselves, they would have stopped such a prayer as impious and told him to ask for those things from the Lord, not from them. Are we to think, then, that what they would have rejected as impious and sacrilegious while they lived on earth can please them now?

lemmas.gloss: yet he would not be tolerated

choices.term: Angustum per iter scandere largiens Dona regna perennia
choices.english: You who grant us to climb the narrow road, give us the everlasting kingdom
choices.why: Dona is the imperative 'give', parallel to the other petitions, not the noun 'gifts'.

notes: The Benedict line alludes to the narrow way of Matthew 7:14.

sections.title: Some prayers even ask the saints to act by their own delegated power and command
sections.pass_a: Add that in the usage of the Roman Church not a few prayers directed to the Saints are found, in which not only are goods of Grace and Glory asked of them, but they are also asked that they furnish them to us by the power handed over to them, and by their command and precept. Which is plainly another thing than to obtain such goods for us from God by their prayers. As when it is said to the Apostles in common, You who shut heaven by a word, And loose its bolts, Loose us from all sins, By your command, we beseech. To whose precept is subjected, Health and sickness of all, Heal those sick in morals, Restoring us to virtues. Again, Order us guilty, we beseech, To be loosed from guilt. And specially to the Apostle Peter, Loose the chains of sin By the power handed to thee, By which thou shuttest heaven to all by a Word, and openest. As was also proved more fully by us above.
pass_b: Besides, in the usage of the Roman Church there are quite a few prayers addressed to the saints in which they are asked not only for the goods of grace and glory, but also to give these to us by the power entrusted to them, by their own order and command. That is plainly something other than obtaining such goods for us from God by their prayers.

So the apostles together are addressed: "You who shut heaven by your word and loose its bolts, loose us from all our sins by your command, we pray." And: "Health and sickness of all are subject to your command; heal those sick in their ways, restoring us to virtue." And again: "Command that we, guilty men, be loosed from our guilt, we pray." And to the Apostle Peter in particular: "By the power given you, loose the chains of sin, you who by your word shut heaven to all and open it."
We proved this more fully above as well.

lemmas.gloss: by the power entrusted to them
by their own order and command

choices.term: Quorum praecepto subditur, Salus & languor omnium
choices.english: Health and sickness of all are subject to your command
choices.why: Subditur is the verb of the hymn line; the English joins it to its subject as the hymn does.
rejected: It is added by their precept

notes: The first lines to the apostles are from the breviary hymn Exultet caelum laudibus.

sections.title: Mutual prayer among the living gives no warrant for invoking the departed
sections.pass_a: Even if indeed the Roman Church asked nothing else of the Saints than that they pray to God for us, yet that could by no means be defended as lawful by the example of those prayers which the faithful ask from one another; when namely, pressed by some necessity, they ask their brothers that they be willing to help them with God by the aid of their prayers. For from the fact that in Scripture we are admonished both to help our brothers with prayers, and to ask such mutual help from them, it does not follow that someone living in Europe can, without folly, or even impiety, address with mouth or heart a holy man dwelling among the Chinese or the Americans, and ask him as if seeing and hearing that he intercede with God for him, and obtain what he feels he needs. How then shall we conclude from it that we can piously and with reason ask of Saints departed in Christ, either by voice, or even by the sole affection of the heart, that they pray to God for us; when they, already carried up into the heavenly paradise, are as far from us as the highest heaven from the earth; nor does any commerce remain to us with them, until we enjoy a like blessedness; and means of communicating mutual thoughts? Therefore from the prayers which the faithful, warring together on earth, ask of one another, it no more follows that the Saints already received into heaven can be invoked by us, than it formerly followed, according to the doctrine of the Roman Church, that the souls of the fathers detained in Limbo were to be invoked by the faithful living at that time.
pass_b: Even if the Roman Church asked nothing of the saints except that they pray to God for us, that could not be defended as lawful by the example of the prayers believers ask of one another, when under some need they ask their brothers to help them before God with their prayers.

Scripture tells us both to help our brothers with our prayers and to ask the same help from them. It does not follow that someone living in Europe could, without folly or even impiety, speak aloud or in his heart to a holy man living among the Chinese or in the Americas, ask him as if he could see and hear to intercede with God for him, and obtain what he feels he needs.

How then can we conclude from it that we may piously and reasonably ask the saints who have died in Christ, aloud or only in the heart's desire, to pray to God for us? They have been carried up into the heavenly paradise and are as far from us as the highest heaven is from the earth. Until we enjoy the same blessedness, we have no dealings with them and no means of sharing our thoughts.

So from the prayers that believers fighting side by side on earth ask of one another, it no more follows that we may invoke the saints already received into heaven than it once followed, on the Roman Church's own teaching, that the believers then living should have invoked the souls of the fathers held in Limbo.

choices.english: fighting side by side on earth
choices.why: Echoes the church militant without importing the later technical phrase.

notes: The 1675 print reads 'non aliud a Sanctis petere' where sense needs 'peteret'; the English follows the sense ('asked').

sections.title: Rome assumes the saints see and hear all who pray to them; that is walking in what we have not seen
sections.pass_a: The Theologians of the Roman School indeed suppose that the Spirits of the just admitted into heaven, notwithstanding so great a distance of places, know and perceive the things which are done on earth; and that each one of the Saints can at the same time not only hear the prayers of all men invoking them, and see their necessities, but also behold the inmost thoughts and secret affections of the heart, and know them certainly. But this ought not to have been supposed without the word of God, and certain reason: and to pronounce it from our conjectures and suspicions is plainly to set foot in the things which we have not seen.
pass_b: The theologians of the Roman school assume that the spirits of the just, once admitted into heaven, know and perceive what happens on earth despite so vast a distance. They assume that each saint can at one and the same time hear the prayers of everyone who calls on him and see their needs, and can also look into their inmost thoughts and the hidden desires of their hearts and know them with certainty.

But this should not have been assumed without the word of God and sure reasoning. To declare it on the strength of our guesses and suspicions is simply to set foot in things we have not seen (Colossians 2:18).

lemmas.gloss: the hidden desires of the heart

choices.term: pedem inferre in ea quae non vidimus
choices.english: to set foot in things we have not seen
choices.why: Le Blanc turns Colossians 2:18 back on his opponents; the English keeps the same image as in LXXXIII.

sections.title: The burden of proof lies on those who claim the saints hear us
sections.pass_a: Nor is it ours to prove the contrary; although many things could be brought from Scripture on this matter. For that we should abstain from imploring the prayers and suffrages of departed Saints, it suffices that we do not know whether they hear us; nor see that revealed in the Word of God. But on those who affirm that the matter is so, it is incumbent to prove what they say; and the knowledge of our affairs which they attribute to the souls of the Saints they are bound to demonstrate by an invincible argument, or by some clear oracle of Scripture. Otherwise that devotion of theirs toward the pious souls of the Saints will wholly totter, and will be done without faith.
pass_b: Nor is it our task to prove the contrary, though much could be brought from Scripture on the point. For us to refrain from begging the prayers and suffrages of departed saints, it is enough that we do not know whether they hear us and do not find it revealed in God's word.

Those who say it is so must prove what they say. They are bound to demonstrate the knowledge of our affairs that they ascribe to the souls of the saints, by an argument that cannot be answered or by some clear word of Scripture. Otherwise their devotion toward the holy souls of the saints will totter altogether and be practiced without faith.

choices.english: be practiced without faith
choices.why: Le Blanc means without the warrant of faith (Romans 14:23 sense), not insincerely.

sections.title: Prophets and apostles knew hidden things by revelation for their office; it does not follow the dead see all
sections.pass_a: But how weak and light are the things which they bring from Scripture to make faith in so great a matter will easily appear to one shaking them out. First then that the Saints reigning with Christ in the heavens know the things which are done on earth, and therefore perceive the prayers of all who invoke them, and behold their thoughts and hearts, they prove from this that some living men were not ignorant of absent and future things; and so of the hidden things of the heart. As, for example, Elisha, who said to his servant Gehazi, Was not my Heart present, when the man came down from his chariot to meet thee? And Samuel who said to Saul, All things that are in thy heart I will tell thee; and of the asses of thy Father, which thou lost. And so Peter absent knew that Ananias and Sapphira had defrauded of the price of the field. And Paul looking at the heart of the lame beggar, knew that he had faith, to be made whole. But what kind of consequence is this, Prophets and Apostles knew certain hidden things, which pertained to their office, God revealing: therefore the souls of the Blessed, received into heavenly glory, know the things which are done on earth, and see the necessities of all who invoke them, and perceive their prayers, conceived either by mouth, or by the heart alone and affection? From it indeed it follows that God can reveal to the Blessed Spirits of the just whatever necessities, actions, and thoughts of men living here he pleases; but whether he does it, or not, can in no way be concluded from it. 2 Kings 5. 1 Samuel 9. Acts 5. Acts 14.
pass_b: Anyone who sifts the proofs they bring from Scripture to establish so great a matter will easily see how weak and light they are.

First, they prove that the saints reigning with Christ in heaven know what happens on earth, and so hear the prayers of all who call on them and see into their thoughts and hearts, from the fact that some men while still alive knew things absent and future, and even the secrets of the heart. Elisha, for example, said to his servant Gehazi, "Did not my heart go with you when the man came down from his chariot to meet you?" (2 Kings 5:26). Samuel said to Saul, "I will tell you all that is in your heart," and spoke of his father's asses that he had lost (1 Samuel 9:19-20). Peter knew, though he was not present, that Ananias and Sapphira had kept back part of the price of the field (Acts 5:1-9). Paul looked into the heart of the lame beggar and saw that he had faith to be healed (Acts 14:9).

But what sort of inference is this: prophets and apostles knew certain hidden things that belonged to their office, because God revealed them; therefore the souls of the blessed, received into heavenly glory, know what happens on earth, see the needs of all who call on them, and hear their prayers, whether spoken aloud or formed only in the heart's desire? What does follow is that God can reveal to the blessed spirits of the just whatever needs, actions and thoughts of men living here he pleases. Whether he does so cannot be concluded from it at all.

lemmas.gloss: to one who sifts, shakes out

choices.english: Peter knew, though he was not present
choices.why: Le Blanc's absens refers to what Peter knew of a transaction he had not witnessed; the English keeps his claim without correcting it.

notes: The 1675 margin gives chapters only (2 Reg. 5; 1 Sam. 9; Act. 5; Act. 14); the English supplies verses.

sections.title: Appeal to the saints' office as patrons proves the unknown by the equally unknown
sections.pass_a: But if anyone says that the office entrusted by God to the departed Saints requires that they have knowledge of our affairs, because namely they have been constituted by God our Patrons and intercessors, he proves the unknown by the equally unknown. For the word of God nowhere teaches that the Saints enjoying heavenly glory have been given to us by God as guardians and Mediators, who intercede for us with God: rather the contrary is gathered quite evidently from sacred Scripture. Nor can it be said that it pertains to the blessedness of the Saints that they hear the prayers of those invoking them, because namely this makes for their greater glory. For if the invocation of Saints departed in Christ is a superstitious and unlawful thing, and devised only by men, it in no way pertains to the glory of the Saints that they know who invoke them: and it ought first to have been proved that it is pleasing and acceptable to God that the Saints reigning with him be invoked, before it is supposed with any appearance of probability that such invocation makes for their glory.
pass_b: Suppose someone says that the office God has given the departed saints requires them to know our affairs, since God has appointed them our patrons and intercessors. He proves the unknown by what is just as unknown.

God's word nowhere teaches that the saints who enjoy heavenly glory have been given us by God as guardians and mediators to intercede for us with him. On the contrary, the opposite is gathered quite clearly from Scripture.

Nor can it be said that hearing the prayers of those who call on them belongs to the saints' blessedness on the ground that it adds to their glory. If calling on the saints who have died in Christ is superstitious and unlawful, a human invention, then knowing who calls on them adds nothing to the saints' glory. It ought first to have been proved that God is pleased and accepts it when the saints who reign with him are invoked, before anyone could suppose with any show of probability that such invocation adds to their glory.

lemmas.gloss: proves the unknown by the equally unknown

choices.english: with any show of probability
choices.why: Species is 'appearance'; Le Blanc denies the claim even a surface plausibility.

sections.title: Rome's proof from Matthew 22 and Luke 15: the just are equal to angels, and angels know sinners' repentance
sections.pass_a: Moreover, that the Saints triumphing in heaven are not ignorant of what men do, and of what befalls them in this lower world; nay, that the thoughts of men are not hidden from them, the Theologians of the Roman School prove from this, that these things do not escape the knowledge of Angels. For Christ himself testifies that the just will be in the heavens isangelous, as the Angels of God; in Matthew chapter twenty-two. And therefore since they must be equal to Angels, it is not to be thought that they are surpassed by Angels in the knowledge of our affairs. Now that the things done on earth are known to the heavenly Angels, and so the very inner motions and affections of human hearts, they think follows from the fact that they are said to rejoice over one sinner doing penance, more than over ninety-nine just. For if the penitence of sinners is perceived by them, surely they know what is done in the world; not only outwardly, but also inwardly in the heart of the sinner, in which is true penitence and sorrow for Sins. Luke 15:10.
pass_b: The theologians of the Roman school also argue that the saints triumphant in heaven are not ignorant of what men do or of what happens to them in this lower world, and that even men's thoughts are not hidden from them, because these things do not escape the knowledge of the angels.

For Christ himself testifies that the just in heaven will be "equal to the angels" (isangeloi), "as the angels of God," in the twenty-second chapter of Matthew (Matthew 22:30; compare Luke 20:36). Since they are to be equal to the angels, they argue, we must not think that angels surpass them in knowledge of our affairs.

And they take it to follow that what happens on earth, even the inner movements and feelings of human hearts, is known to the angels of heaven, because the angels are said to rejoice "over one sinner who repents more than over ninety-nine righteous persons" (Luke 15:7, 10). If the angels see sinners' repentance, they certainly know what happens in the world, not only outwardly but inwardly too, in the sinner's heart, where true repentance and sorrow for sin reside.

choices.english: the saints triumphant in heaven
choices.why: The church-triumphant phrase is Le Blanc's own antithesis to 'militant' in XCV.

notes: Isangeloi is Luke 20:36; Matthew 22:30 has 'as the angels of God'. The words about ninety-nine just are Luke 15:7, joined to the angels of 15:10 (the margin gives Luc. 15. 10).

sections.title: Angels serve us by office and so know our repentance; nothing shows the dead have that office. Pars Secunda closes
sections.pass_a: But it is not wonderful that Angels, who are ministering spirits sent into ministry for those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation, since by office they are present with us, and are occupied about us, know the things which pertain to us, and above all the penitence and conversion of sinners, to procuring which they serve by God's mandate: but, as we have already said, that a similar office has been entrusted by God to the blessed souls of the just cannot be shown from the word of God. Nor does it bear on this what Christ affirms, that the just will be in heaven isangelous. For this equality or likeness with Angels ought not to be extended beyond Christ's scope; which is to teach that the just after the resurrection will lead an Angelic life, inasmuch as they will no longer be subject to the necessities and infirmities of this life, and will neither marry, nor be given in marriage, as is plain to one reading the words of Christ in Matthew. Add that it does not follow that individual Angels know the thoughts of individual men, and perceive their prayers, from the fact that Christ indefinitely says that there is joy to the Angels on account of the conversion of one sinner. Just as we can truly say that there is great joy in the Church of God, when one sinner is converted to God; Yet it does not follow from that, that to each one who is in the Church the thoughts, words and deeds of all the others are known. Hebrews 1:13.
pass_b: It is no wonder that angels, who are "ministering spirits sent to serve for the sake of those who will inherit salvation" (Hebrews 1:14), know what concerns us, above all the repentance and conversion of sinners, which they are commanded by God to help bring about. Their office keeps them with us and about us. But, as we have already said, it cannot be shown from God's word that God has entrusted a like office to the blessed souls of the just.

Nor is Christ's saying that the just will be "equal to the angels" in heaven to the point. That equality or likeness to the angels must not be stretched beyond Christ's purpose, which is to teach that after the resurrection the just will live the life of angels, in that they will no longer be subject to the needs and weaknesses of this life and will neither marry nor be given in marriage, as anyone who reads Christ's words in Matthew can see (Matthew 22:30).

Further, when Christ says in general terms that there is joy among the angels over the conversion of one sinner, it does not follow that each angel knows each man's thoughts and hears his prayers. In the same way we can truly say that there is great joy in the Church of God when one sinner turns to God, and yet it does not follow that every member of the Church knows the thoughts, words and deeds of all the others.

choices.english: their office keeps them with us
choices.why: Ex officio grounds the angels' knowledge in their assigned task, which is Le Blanc's whole contrast with the dead.

notes: The 1675 margin reads Heb. 1. 13; the words quoted are Hebrews 1:14, so the English gives 1:14.
